title: A piston-like polymer stochastic heat engine
abstract: Colloidal stochastic engines are often regarded as microscopic analogues of macroscopic pis ton cylinder heat engines. However, although they share some underlying physical principles, such systems remain far from being direct force generators from a practical perspective. Motivated by this limitation, the present study introduces a polymer-based stochastic engine that more closely mimics the operation of piston cylinder engines. In this setup, heat is converted into work through a cyclic process in which a polymer is pulled into and out of a narrow channel under varying tem peratures. The work performed by the engine can be directly obtained from the cyclic trajectory in the force position diagram, analogous to the pressure volume diagram in traditional heat engines. Despite its much higher number of degrees of freedom compared to colloidal engines, the polymer en gine nevertheless follows several characteristic features observed in such systems. Numerical results demonstrate consistency with universal low-dissipation bounds for e ciency, recovery of Carnot e ciency under regeneration, and low-dissipation scaling of work and power.
summary: The authors introduce and analyze a novel stochastic heat engine based on polymer confinement that more closely mimics classical piston engines. By simulating cyclic work extraction under varying temperatures, they demonstrate the recovery of fundamental thermodynamic limits, such as Carnot efficiency, while also mapping out finite-time performance boundaries.
main_problem: To develop a stochastic heat engine model that more accurately mimics macroscopic piston-cylinder engines compared to existing colloidal analogues, allowing for direct work calculation from the force-position diagram.
main_result: The polymer-based engine successfully demonstrates characteristic features of thermal machines, recovering Carnot efficiency under ideal regeneration and following universal low-dissipation bounds in finite-time analysis.
method: The study uses both theoretical quasistatic cycle definitions (e.g., Jarzynski equality) and numerical simulations involving Langevin dynamics to calculate work, power, and efficiency across various driving speeds.
model_or_system: The system is a polymer chain confined in a narrow channel, modeled using bead-spring interactions governed by an overdamped Langevin equation. Work extraction occurs via cyclic processes involving isothermal contraction (cold) and retraction (hot).
key_observables: Cycle work ($W_{	ext{cyc}}$), power ($P_{	ext{cyc}}$), efficiency ($\eta$), free energy change ($\Delta F$), and the force magnitude during isothermal strokes.
important_parameters: Temperatures ($T_c=300$ K, $T_h=350$ K), channel width ($d/l$), cycle time ($	au_{	ext{cyc}}$), and coupling constants ($k_s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the plateau approximation for the recoil force during isothermal strokes, and finite-time results are compared against low-dissipation theoretical bounds.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the engine cycle (force-position diagram), free energy reconstruction via Jarzynski equality, and plots showing work, power, and efficiency dependence on total cycle time ($	au_{	ext{cyc}}$) and temperature.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by defining the polymer engine cycle and calculating quasistatic limits. It then proceeds to numerical simulations, validating force measurements using iso-force analysis and analyzing finite-time performance across various driving speeds to map out power-efficiency trade-offs.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, mesoscopic realization of non-equilibrium thermodynamics principles (like the Jarzynski equality) in a polymer system, offering insights into how complex molecular dynamics can govern macroscopic energy conversion processes relevant to statistical mechanics.
